  1. 1

    What is the leading coefficient of p(x)=7−4x2+x5−9x3p(x) = 7 - 4x^2 + x^5 - 9x^3p(x)=7−4x2+x5−9x3?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the coefficient of the first term as printed, before putting the polynomial into standard form.

    You chose B: Chooses the coefficient of largest size rather than the one attached to the highest power.

    You chose D: Reports the degree, which is the exponent on the leading term, not the number multiplying it.

    Order the terms by descending power first; nothing may be read off until that is done.

    p(x)=x5−9x3−4x2+7p(x) = x^5 - 9x^3 - 4x^2 + 7p(x)=x5−9x3−4x2+7

    The highest power present is x5x^5x5, and the number sitting on it is 111, so the leading coefficient is 111.

    What is the remainder when x3+6x2−4x^3 + 6x^2 - 4x3+6x2−4 is divided by x−1x - 1x−1?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reports the constant term, which is the value at 000 rather than at the input that makes the divisor zero.

    You chose C: Adds only the coefficients of the terms carrying an xxx, leaving the constant term out of the sum.

    You chose D: Uses −1-1−1 as the corner value, which belongs to the divisor x+1x + 1x+1; the value that makes x−1x - 1x−1 zero is 111.

    The remainder on dividing by x−1x - 1x−1 is the value of the polynomial at the input that makes x−1x - 1x−1 zero, namely 111.

    P(1)=13+6(1)2−4=1+6−4=3P(1) = 1^3 + 6(1)^2 - 4 = 1 + 6 - 4 = 3P(1)=13+6(1)2−4=1+6−4=3

    The missing xxx term contributes nothing, and the constant term −4-4−4 is included with its sign.

  3. 3

    A polynomial of degree 999 is divided by a polynomial of degree 444, and the remainder is not the zero polynomial. What is the degree of the quotient, and what is the greatest degree the remainder can have?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Lets the remainder reach the divisor's own degree; the loop stops only once the degree has fallen strictly below it.

    You chose B: Gives the quotient the divisor's degree instead of the difference of the two degrees.

    You chose C: Adds the two degrees, as a product would, where a division subtracts them.

    In P=DQ+RP = DQ + RP=DQ+R the product DQDQDQ must match the dividend's leading term, so the degrees subtract, and the loop runs until the leftover's degree drops below the divisor's.

    deg⁡Q=9−4=5,deg⁡R≤3\deg Q = 9 - 4 = 5, \qquad \deg R \le 3degQ=9−4=5,degR≤3

    A remainder of degree 444 would still contain a whole copy of the divisor, so the division would not be finished.

    Solution

    You chose A: Rejects a candidate for being negative, but every entry on the list carries both signs.

    You chose C: Rejects a denominator larger than its numerator, but the denominator is tested against the leading coefficient alone, and 666 divides 666.

    You chose D: Rejects an integer as large as the constant term itself, but an integer candidate need only divide that term, and 141414 divides 141414.

    In lowest terms, a rational root pq\tfrac{p}{q}qp​ needs ppp dividing the constant term 141414 and qqq dividing the leading coefficient 666.

    p∈{1,2,7,14},q∈{1,2,3,6}p \in \{1, 2, 7, 14\}, \qquad q \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\}p∈{1,2,7,14},q∈{1,2,3,6}

    The number 43\tfrac{4}{3}34​ has numerator 444, and 444 does not divide 141414, so it cannot be a root. The other three pass both tests, which makes them candidates and nothing more.

    No number on the candidate list of P(x)=x3+x−5P(x) = x^3 + x - 5P(x)=x3+x−5 is a root of it, and P(1)=−3P(1) = -3P(1)=−3 while P(2)=5P(2) = 5P(2)=5. Which statement is correct?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Supposes the list can overlook a rational root; the theorem guarantees that every rational root, in lowest terms, appears on it.

    You chose B: Reads a failed candidate list as ruling out real roots. The list holds only fractions, so it can rule out nothing else.

    You chose C: Leaves open a question already closed: a rational root of PPP would have to be ±1\pm 1±1 or ±5\pm 5±5, and none of those is one.

    The sign change locates a real root, and the failed list decides what kind of number it is.

    P(1)=−3<0<5=P(2)P(1) = -3 < 0 < 5 = P(2)P(1)=−3<0<5=P(2)

    So a real root sits strictly between 111 and 222. Since PPP is monic with constant term −5-5−5, any rational root would be an integer dividing 555, and all four of ±1\pm 1±1 and ±5\pm 5±5 have been tested and failed. A real root that cannot be rational is irrational.

Which interval must contain a real zero of hhh, and what do the values at 333 and 444 establish about the interval between them?

    Answer choices for question 18

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Treats matching signs as a guarantee in the other direction. A curve can dip below the axis and return, meeting it twice between two inputs of the same sign.

    You chose C: Reads outputs climbing toward zero as reaching it; −13-13−13 and −2-2−2 both still sit below the axis, so nothing is forced there.

    You chose D: Picks the interval with the largest jump in output, 313131 to 989898, mistaking a steep climb for a crossing.

    Take the two halves in turn. For the first, look for a neighbouring pair in the table whose sign changes.

    h(2)=−2<0<31=h(3)h(2) = -2 < 0 < 31 = h(3)h(2)=−2<0<31=h(3)

    The pair at 333 and 444 is a different matter. So that pair leaves the question open rather than closing it, and the same holds for h(0)h(0)h(0) with h(1)h(1)h(1), and for h(1)h(1)h(1) with h(2)h(2)h(2).

      The second polynomial, GGG, has degree 666 and its graph crosses the horizontal axis at six different points. Decide how many turning points that graph must have, giving both the largest and the smallest number the description allows, and name the fact that supplies each bound.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    FFF has degree 555, leading term 2x52x^52x5 and constant term −315-315−315.

    • the leading term may be written 2x52x^52x5 or as the coefficient 222 on x5x^5x5; 18x518x^518x5 is not the same, since the repeated factor contributes x2x^2x2 and not 32x23^2x^232x2

    Part B

    The graph falls on the far left and rises on the far right. FFF has two distinct real zeros, −3-3−3 from the repeated factor and 72\tfrac{7}{2}27​ from 2x−72x - 72x−7; the factor x2+5x^2 + 5x2+5 is never zero, so it contributes none.

    Part C

    Exactly five. The degree caps the turning points at 6−1=56 - 1 = 56−1=5, and six distinct real zeros force at least 6−1=56 - 1 = 56−1=5 of them, so the two bounds meet and no other count is possible.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Degrees add across a product and leading terms multiply, so the factored form gives up all three answers with no expansion.

    deg⁡F=2+1+2=5,(x2)(2x)(x2)=2x5\deg F = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, \qquad \left(x^2\right)(2x)\left(x^2\right) = 2x^5degF=2+1+2=5,(x2)(2x)(x2)=2x5

    The constant term is the value at x=0x = 0x=0, which is the product of the factors' own constants:

    F(0)=(3)2(−7)(5)=9×(−35)=−315.F(0) = (3)^2(-7)(5) = 9 \times (-35) = -315.F(0)=(3)2(−7)(5)=9×(−35)=−315.

    Part B

    The far ends belong to the leading term alone, which part A found to be 2x52x^52x5: an odd degree with a positive leading coefficient, so the graph falls on the far left and rises on the far right.

    A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is, so take the factors one at a time:

    (x+3)2=0 ⇒ x=−3,2x−7=0 ⇒ x=72,x2+5≥5>0.(x + 3)^2 = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ x = -3, \qquad 2x - 7 = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ x = \tfrac{7}{2}, \qquad x^2 + 5 \ge 5 > 0.(x+3)2=0 ⇒ x=−3,2x−7=0 ⇒ x=27​,x2+5≥5>0.

    The squared factor supplies the single number −3-3−3 however many times it appears, and x2+5x^2 + 5x2+5 never reaches zero for a real input. So there are two distinct real zeros, comfortably inside the ceiling of 555 that degree 555 allows.

    Part C

    Two separate facts press on the count from opposite sides.

    From above. A polynomial of degree nnn has a graph with at most n−1n - 1n−1 turning points, so

    #{turning points}≤6−1=5.\#\{\text{turning points}\} \le 6 - 1 = 5.#{turning points}≤6−1=5.

    From below. Between two neighbouring zeros the graph leaves the axis and comes back to it, so it must stop rising or stop falling somewhere in between. Six distinct zeros have five neighbouring pairs, each forcing at least one turning point:

    #{turning points}≥6−1=5.\#\{\text{turning points}\} \ge 6 - 1 = 5.#{turning points}≥6−1=5.

    The two bounds are the same number, so the count is pinned: exactly five. Note how differently the two arguments work. The ceiling is a fact about degree and holds whatever the zeros do; the floor is a fact about the zeros and would collapse if any two of the six coincided, since only distinct zeros have a stretch of graph between them.

    In one line

    F(x)=(x+3)2(2x−7)(x2+5)F(x) = (x + 3)^2(2x - 7)\left(x^2 + 5\right)F(x)=(x+3)2(2x−7)(x2+5) has degree 555, leading term 2x52x^52x5 and constant term −315-315−315, so its graph falls on the far left and rises on the far right. It has two distinct real zeros, −3-3−3 and 72\tfrac{7}{2}27​, since x2+5x^2 + 5x2+5 never vanishes and a repeated factor still names one number. The graph of GGG must have exactly five turning points: degree 666 allows at most 555, and six distinct real zeros force at least 555, so the ceiling and the floor meet.

    The answer

    Part A

    P(x)=2x4−7x3+9x−4P(x) = 2x^4 - 7x^3 + 9x - 4P(x)=2x4−7x3+9x−4. It is the only possible dividend because PPP is computed from DDD, QQQ and RRR rather than chosen.

    Part B

    All but x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4. A remainder must be the zero polynomial or have degree below the divisor's degree 222, so 777 (degree 000), 6x−116x - 116x−11 (degree 111) and 000 all qualify, while x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4 has degree 222 and still contains a whole copy of DDD.

    The quotient is 000 and the remainder is 4x−94x - 94x−9. That pair keeps the identity and keeps the degree condition, since deg⁡(4x−9)=1<2\deg(4x - 9) = 1 < 2deg(4x−9)=1<2, and only one pair can keep both, so it is the answer.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The division algorithm's identity runs in both directions, so multiply back.

    (x2−3x+1)(2x2−x−5)=2x4−7x3+0x2+14x−5\left(x^2 - 3x + 1\right)\left(2x^2 - x - 5\right) = 2x^4 - 7x^3 + 0x^2 + 14x - 5(x2−3x+1)(2x2−x−5)=2x4−7x3+0x2+14x−5

    Collecting that product: 2x42x^42x4 from the leading pair; −x3−6x3=−7x3-x^3 - 6x^3 = -7x^3−x3−6x3=−7x3; −5x2+3x2+2x2=0-5x^2 + 3x^2 + 2x^2 = 0−5x2+3x2+2x2=0; 15x−x=14x15x - x = 14x15x−x=14x; and −5-5−5. Now add the remainder:

    P(x)=2x4−7x3+0x2+14x−5+(−5x+1)=2x4−7x3+9x−4.P(x) = 2x^4 - 7x^3 + 0x^2 + 14x - 5 + (-5x + 1) = 2x^4 - 7x^3 + 9x - 4.P(x)=2x4−7x3+0x2+14x−5+(−5x+1)=2x4−7x3+9x−4.

    Uniqueness is not even needed here. The right-hand side DQ+RDQ + RDQ+R is a single polynomial once the three are fixed, so there is nothing left to choose.

    Part B

    The divisor has degree 222, so the stopping condition reads: the remainder is the zero polynomial, or its degree is at most 111.

    R=0ordeg⁡R<deg⁡D=2R = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad \deg R < \deg D = 2R=0ordegR<degD=2

    Taking them in turn: 777 has degree 000, so it passes; 6x−116x - 116x−11 has degree 111, so it passes; 000 is named separately by the condition, since the zero polynomial has no degree at all, and it passes. That leaves x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4, whose degree is 222, exactly the divisor's. It is disqualified, and the reason is visible rather than formal: one more copy of DDD can still be taken out of it, since

    x2+4=(x2−3x+1)+(3x+3),x^2 + 4 = \left(x^2 - 3x + 1\right) + (3x + 3),x2+4=(x2−3x+1)+(3x+3),

    which moves a 111 into the quotient and leaves 3x+33x + 33x+3, a genuine remainder. A leftover that still contains a copy of the divisor is an unfinished division, not the answer to one.

    Part C

    Test the candidate pair Q=0Q = 0Q=0 and R=4x−9R = 4x - 9R=4x−9 against the two promises.

    4x−9=(x2−3x+1)⋅0+(4x−9),deg⁡(4x−9)=1<2=deg⁡D4x - 9 = \left(x^2 - 3x + 1\right)\cdot 0 + (4x - 9), \qquad \deg(4x - 9) = 1 < 2 = \deg D4x−9=(x2−3x+1)⋅0+(4x−9),deg(4x−9)=1<2=degD

    The identity holds trivially, and the degree condition holds because a linear leftover is already smaller, in degree, than a quadratic divisor. Uniqueness closes the argument: the division algorithm promises exactly one pair keeping both conditions, so any pair that keeps both is that pair. The loop agrees without being run, because its stopping test is already satisfied before the first pass, and the corresponding integer statement is the familiar one that 333 divided by 555 gives quotient 000 and remainder 333.

    Watch out. A quotient of 000 is a finished answer, not a failure to divide. Nothing in the algorithm promises the quotient is nonzero.

Of the four proposed leftovers, 777, 6x−116x - 116x−11 and 000 are legal remainders for this divisor while x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4 is not, because it still contains a whole copy of DDD. Dividing 4x−94x - 94x−9 by the same divisor gives quotient 000 and remainder 4x−94x - 94x−9: that pair keeps the identity and the degree condition, and uniqueness makes anything keeping both the answer.

    10. A crate that has to hold thirty cubic metres . 18 points. Question 10 of 10.

    18 pts

    A rectangular crate is built to a single dial setting xxx, measured in metres. Its height is xxx metres, its base is 2x−12x - 12x−1 metres wide and x+3x + 3x+3 metres long, and the crate is required to hold exactly 303030 cubic metres.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Express the crate's volume as a polynomial in xxx in standard form. Then rearrange the thirty cubic metre requirement so that one side reads zero and every coefficient is a whole number, and say which values of xxx describe a crate that could actually be built.

      Model the situation Name your unknown first, then write every other quantity in terms of that one letter. 6 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the height, then give all three measurements in metres. Say also how large the permitted set of fractions is, and how much of it your part A restriction throws away.

      Carry your own answer forward Build the candidate list from the equation you wrote in part A, whatever it was, and prune it with your own restriction on xxx.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 6 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Take the linear factor supplied by the height you found out of the equation, then use the polynomial that remains to decide whether a second value of xxx could meet the requirement. Say what your decision settles about the crate.

      Carry your own answer forward Work from the height you reported in part B, whatever it was, and reason about the quotient that your own division leaves behind.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    V(x)=2x3+5x2−3xV(x) = 2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3xV(x)=2x3+5x2−3x, so the requirement is 2x3+5x2−3x−30=02x^3 + 5x^2 - 3x - 30 = 02x3+5x2−3x−30=0. The crate exists only for x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​, since the width 2x−12x - 12x−1 must be positive.

    Part B

    The height is x=2x = 2x=2 metres, so the crate is 222 m high on a base 333 m by 555 m. The theorem permits 242424 candidates, of which 111111 clear x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​.

    • the three measurements may be given in any order as 222 m, 333 m and 555 m; a height of 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​ would give a volume of 555555 cubic metres, not 303030

    Part C

    Dividing leaves 2x2+9x+152x^2 + 9x + 152x2+9x+15, whose discriminant 81−120=−3981 - 120 = -3981−120=−39 is negative, so it has no real roots. The equation therefore has x=2x = 2x=2 as its only real solution, and no second crate of these proportions holds 303030 cubic metres.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Volume is height times width times length, so multiply the three given measurements.

    V(x)=x(2x−1)(x+3)=x(2x2+5x−3)=2x3+5x2−3xV(x) = x(2x - 1)(x + 3) = x\left(2x^2 + 5x - 3\right) = 2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3xV(x)=x(2x−1)(x+3)=x(2x2+5x−3)=2x3+5x2−3x

    Setting that equal to 303030 and moving everything to one side gives the equation the theorem can read:

    2x3+5x2−3x−30=0.2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3x - 30 = 0.2x3+5x2−3x−30=0.

    Moving the 303030 across is what supplies a nonzero constant term. The volume polynomial itself has constant term 000, on which the numerator condition would say nothing.

    For the restriction, all three measurements must be positive: x>0x > 0x>0, 2x−1>02x - 1 > 02x−1>0 and x+3>0x + 3 > 0x+3>0. The middle one is the binding condition, so the situation allows exactly x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​.

    Part B

    The constant term is −30-30−30 and the leading coefficient is 222, so numerators divide 303030 and denominators divide 222:

    ±1, ±2, ±3, ±5, ±6, ±10, ±15, ±30, ±12, ±32, ±52, ±152\pm 1, \ \pm 2, \ \pm 3, \ \pm 5, \ \pm 6, \ \pm 10, \ \pm 15, \ \pm 30, \ \pm\tfrac{1}{2}, \ \pm\tfrac{3}{2}, \ \pm\tfrac{5}{2}, \ \pm\tfrac{15}{2}±1, ±2, ±3, ±5, ±6, ±10, ±15, ±30, ±21​, ±23​, ±25​, ±215​

    That is 121212 positive values and their negatives, so 242424 candidates. The restriction x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​ kills every negative one and 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​ itself, leaving 111111.

    Test the small survivors. At x=1x = 1x=1 the left side is 2+5−3−30=−262 + 5 - 3 - 30 = -262+5−3−30=−26, and at x=2x = 2x=2:

    2(8)+5(4)−6−30=16+20−36=0.2(8) + 5(4) - 6 - 30 = 16 + 20 - 36 = 0.2(8)+5(4)−6−30=16+20−36=0.

    So the height is 222 metres, the width is 2(2)−1=32(2) - 1 = 32(2)−1=3 metres and the length is 2+3=52 + 3 = 52+3=5 metres. The volume checks: 2×3×5=302 \times 3 \times 5 = 302×3×5=30 cubic metres.

    Part C

    Run the tableau with corner 222 on the coefficients 2,  5,  −3,  −302,\; 5,\; -3,\; -302,5,−3,−30. The bottom row is 2,  9,  15,  02,\; 9,\; 15,\; 02,9,15,0, the final 000 re-confirming the root, so

    2x3+5x2−3x−30=(x−2)(2x2+9x+15).2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3x - 30 = (x - 2)\left(2x^2 + 9x + 15\right).2x3+5x2−3x−30=(x−2)(2x2+9x+15).

    A quadratic quotient ends the hunt. Its discriminant is

    92−4(2)(15)=81−120=−39<0,9^2 - 4(2)(15) = 81 - 120 = -39 < 0,92−4(2)(15)=81−120=−39<0,

    so it has no real roots at all, and in particular none above 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​. The only real solution of the equation is x=2x = 2x=2.

    Read back into the situation, that is a uniqueness statement: the dial setting is forced. There is exactly one crate of these proportions with a volume of 303030 cubic metres, and no second setting, large or small, would have done. Note that the restriction x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​ was not even needed to reach it here, since the quotient offered no competition at all.

    In one line

    The volume is V(x)=x(2x−1)(x+3)=2x3+5x2−3xV(x) = x(2x - 1)(x + 3) = 2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3xV(x)=x(2x−1)(x+3)=2x3+5x2−3x, so the requirement becomes 2x3+5x2−3x−30=02x^3 + 5x^2 - 3x - 30 = 02x3+5x2−3x−30=0 with x>12x > \tfrac{1}{2}x>21​. The theorem permits 242424 candidates, 111111 of which clear the restriction, and x=2x = 2x=2 works: the crate is 222 m high on a base 333 m by 555 m, a volume of 303030 cubic metres. Dividing out x−2x - 2x−2 leaves 2x2+9x+152x^2 + 9x + 152x2+9x+15, whose discriminant 81−120=−3981 - 120 = -3981−120=−39 is negative, so there is no second real solution and the dial setting is unique.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.
